standard.title: Fair Play Rules
standard.description: follow rules to promote fair play in a range of physical activities
standard.prior_knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students bring informal social experience of turn-taking and sharing from play and home contexts. No prior structured engagement with game rules or fair play.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students follow rules in a range of physical activities and can identify what fair and unfair play looks like.

nodes.label: Fair and unfair play
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe actions that would constitute fair and unfair play in minor games.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one example of fair play and one example of unfair play in a game they have participated in.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and describe fair and unfair play actions across a range of minor game contexts; explain why fair play matters to participants.
wider: Explore fair play examples from First Nations Australian games and compare with other game contexts
Discuss scenarios where intent (accidental vs deliberate) affects judgements about fairness
Connect fair play to feelings — how unfair play makes participants feel
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify fair and unfair play lack the conceptual foundation to follow rules purposefully (next node) — they comply mechanically at best. The Y1-2 equivalent (co-constructing rules) requires this conceptual base.

response_modes.reason: Use game stoppages and brief scenario discussions to make fair/unfair distinctions explicit. Foundation students need the concepts named and exemplified concretely before they can apply them.
Varied game contexts — chasing games, target games, cooperative games — reveal that fair play principles are consistent across different rule structures.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Cross-context fair play discussions, including culturally situated examples, build a richer ethical understanding of game participation beyond simple rule compliance.
success_criteria: Names at least one example of fair play and one example of unfair play in a game context
Gives a simple reason why fair play is important (e.g. so everyone can enjoy the game)

nodes.label: Following rules in games
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can demonstrate how to play fairly in a range of minor games and play situations, following rules relating to safety, boundaries and equipment use.
nodes.minimum_width: Follow the rules of one minor game, including safety, boundary and equipment rules, with teacher support.
nodes.typical_width: Demonstrate fair play across a range of minor games; follow safety, boundary and equipment rules consistently; discuss rules when prompted.
wider: Participate in games with varying rule complexity, applying fair play in each
Practise a First Nations Australian game with its specific rules and discuss how the rules promote fair participation
Lead a brief rule explanation for a peer before beginning a game

response_modes.reason: Foundation students need repeated practice following rules across multiple game contexts to internalise fair play as a habit, not just a concept. Consistent, low-stakes practice across diverse games builds rule-following disposition.

success_criteria: Follows the safety, boundary and equipment rules of a minor game during participation
Demonstrates fair play behaviour (e.g. takes turns, respects boundaries, accepts outcomes)
